$comment: Machine-readable index of Open Psychology Interactives.
This file is the single source of truth for what has been published.
When you add a tool, append an entry to the matching module's 'tools'
array. Entry fields follow the metadata standard in CLAUDE.md, so a
tool's own metadata.json and its catalogue entry can be kept identical.
assets/js/main.js renders only entries whose status is exactly
recorded here but does not appear on the site, so a work in progress is
never presented as finished. While a module has no published tools its
page keeps its static 'in preparation' message.
See CONTRIBUTING.md for the field-by-field description.

project.name: Open Psychology Interactives
project.description: Free, accessible, classroom-ready browser-based teaching tools for cognitive psychology, research methods, neuropsychology, social and critical psychology, and personality and individual differences.

modules.summary: Tools for the processes students are asked to take on trust: how attention selects, how memory reconstructs rather than replays, and how perception and judgement are shaped by what the system does with limited capacity.

plannedTopics.title: Selective attention and its costs
plannedTopics.detail: What is missed while attending elsewhere, and why the cost is a property of the task rather than of the person.

plannedTopics.title: Working memory capacity
plannedTopics.detail: Holding, manipulating and losing information, and what the limit does and does not predict.

plannedTopics.title: Reconstructive memory
plannedTopics.detail: How recall is assembled at retrieval, and how confidence and accuracy come apart.

plannedTopics.title: Perception as inference
plannedTopics.detail: Why the same input supports more than one interpretation, and what the system does about it.

plannedTopics.title: Judgement under uncertainty
plannedTopics.detail: Heuristics as a sensible response to limited information rather than as simple error.

modules.summary: Tools for design and inference: how much a statistic moves from sample to sample, what uncertainty around an estimate means, and what a test statistic is actually responding to.

plannedTopics.title: Sampling distributions
plannedTopics.detail: Repeatedly drawing samples from a known population and watching the distribution of the sample mean take shape.

plannedTopics.title: Confidence intervals
plannedTopics.detail: What the interval covers across repeated samples, and what it does not say about a single study.

plannedTopics.title: p-values and significance testing
plannedTopics.detail: How a p-value responds to effect size, sample size and variability, held apart one at a time.

plannedTopics.title: Correlation and regression
plannedTopics.detail: Building a scatterplot point by point to see how outliers, range restriction and non-linearity move the coefficient.

plannedTopics.title: Statistical power
plannedTopics.detail: The trade-off between sample size, effect size and the chance of detecting a real effect.

modules.summary: Tools for brain–behaviour reasoning and the classic experimental tasks, so students can experience the paradigm before they read the effect size.

plannedTopics.title: Classic attention tasks
plannedTopics.detail: Runnable versions of Stroop-type and cueing paradigms, with the student's own data shown afterwards.

plannedTopics.title: Working memory and span
plannedTopics.detail: Span procedures that make the capacity limit something a student meets rather than reads about.

plannedTopics.title: Dissociation logic
plannedTopics.detail: Single and double dissociations, and what each licenses you to conclude about separable processes.

plannedTopics.title: Executive function
plannedTopics.detail: Set-shifting and inhibition tasks, with the switch cost calculated from the student's own responses.

plannedTopics.title: Interpreting deficits
plannedTopics.detail: Why performance on a task rarely maps onto one region, and why network and disconnection accounts are often the better explanation.

modules.summary: Tools for social influence and for the critical questions that follow it: who was studied, what a measure licenses you to claim, and where an empirical pattern ends and an interpretation of it begins.

plannedTopics.title: Conformity and social influence
plannedTopics.detail: How group size, unanimity and private versus public response change the pressure a situation exerts.

plannedTopics.title: Attitudes and what a measure captures
plannedTopics.detail: Why self-report, implicit and behavioural measures of the same attitude often disagree, and what follows from that.

plannedTopics.title: Intergroup bias and its measurement
plannedTopics.detail: What group-level findings support at the level of an individual, and the inferential step that is not licensed.

plannedTopics.title: Sampling, generalisability and WEIRD samples
plannedTopics.detail: Which populations the evidence base was built on, and how that constrains the claims that can be made from it.

plannedTopics.title: Constructing the object of study
plannedTopics.detail: How choosing a definition and a measure shapes the finding, and how contested constructs are handled honestly.

modules.summary: Tools for trait structure and psychological measurement: where factors come from, what reliability and validity buy you, and why an individual profile is harder to interpret than it looks.

plannedTopics.title: Trait structure and the Big Five
plannedTopics.detail: How correlations among many items resolve into a small number of broad dimensions, and what is lost in the reduction.

plannedTopics.title: Factor analysis, made visible
plannedTopics.detail: Watching a correlation matrix reduce to factors, and seeing how the number retained changes the story.

plannedTopics.title: Reliability
plannedTopics.detail: How internal consistency and test–retest reliability respond to scale length and item quality.

plannedTopics.title: Validity and measurement error
plannedTopics.detail: Why an unreliable measure puts a ceiling on the correlation it can show with anything else.

plannedTopics.title: Reading a trait profile
plannedTopics.detail: Norms, percentiles and the standard error of measurement, and how wide the band around a single score really is.

tools.title: Person–Situation Interaction Theatre
tools.summary: Four fictional characters are put through five situations. Students rank their behaviour twice — once where traits show through and once where a different affordance reorders everyone — then take control of situation strength and assigned role to find the setting where the four become behaviourally indistinguishable.
learningObjectives: Explain what makes a situation strong or weak, and what a strong situation does to observed between-person variation.
Distinguish situational constraint from situational affordance, and explain why two equally weak situations can rank the same people differently.
Explain why low observed behavioural variance is not evidence of low trait variance.
Say why neither 'personality matters more' nor 'situations matter more' is a defensible summary of the evidence.
Relate behavioural consistency to aggregation across situations and occasions.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Ranking uses one native select per character rather than drag-and-drop, so there is no dragging to provide an alternative to; duplicate ranks produce an accessible error message rather than a silent failure. Charts and the interaction diagram are hidden from assistive technology and paired with visible tables carrying the same numbers; edge weights are printed as text beside each edge, and negative weights are dashed as well as signed. Keyboard operable throughout; changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Person-situation interaction: situational strength, affordances, and why the debate was badly posed
tools.simulationNotes: Four fictional characters with illustrative trait scores on an arbitrary 0-100 scale; no norms and no reference sample. Behaviour is modelled as k·norm + (1−k)·disposition + role, where k is situation strength and disposition is a weighted sum of only those traits the situation affords. The anonymous-discussion situation carries a negative weight on politeness, which is what reorders the cast. No occasion-to-occasion variability, no measurement error and no trait interactions are modelled. Situation strength is stipulated by the author rather than estimated.

tools.title: State versus Trait Tracker
tools.summary: Simulated experience-sampling data for four fictional people over a fortnight. Students rank them by typical level from a single moment, discover how badly that works, then control within-person variability, measurement error and life events — and watch two people with the same mean turn out to be living quite different fortnights.
learningObjectives: Separate a person's typical level from where they happen to be at one moment.
Explain why within-person variability is a stable characteristic rather than noise to be averaged away.
Explain why measurement error and genuine within-person fluctuation are indistinguishable in one observation and separable across many.
Say how many observations are needed to estimate a person's typical level, and why the answer depends on the person.
Distinguish between-person from within-person variance and interpret the share of variance sitting between people.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Ranking uses native selects rather than drag-and-drop; duplicate ranks produce an accessible error. Four-series line charts distinguish people by colour, by dash pattern and by a name printed at the end of each line, and are hidden from assistive technology in favour of visible tables carrying every summary figure. Sliders announce meaningful values ('measurement error standard deviation 3 points'). The random seed is exposed as a number input so a demonstration is exactly reproducible. Keyboard operable throughout; changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: States versus traits: within-person variability, repeated measurement and what a single administration cannot tell you
tools.simulationNotes: Four fictional people on an arbitrary 0-100 scale with no norms. Each observation is trait + decaying event effect + within-person wobble + measurement error, with wobble drawn from a normal distribution whose SD is a property of the person and error modelled separately so the two can be shown to behave differently under averaging. Randomness uses a seeded mulberry32 generator; the seed is shown and settable, so any dataset is exactly reproducible. Observations are equally spaced with no missingness, no autocorrelation beyond event decay, and no drift in the trait level — all three are unrealistic and are stated as limitations on the page.

tools.title: Factor Rotation Playground
tools.summary: Twelve fictional adjective markers in a two-dimensional factor space. Students rotate the axes and watch every loading change while the configuration of points, each communality and the total variance explained stay exactly where they were — then meet a genuine cross-loading and a pair of clusters that no orthogonal rotation can fit.
learningObjectives: State precisely what rotation changes and what it leaves invariant.
Explain why rotation neither manufactures results nor identifies a uniquely true solution.
Distinguish orthogonal from oblique solutions and treat the choice as a substantive claim about the constructs.
Recognise a genuine cross-loading as information rather than a nuisance.
Defend simple structure as an adopted criterion rather than a discovery.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, select and buttons; rotation is driven by a slider rather than by dragging, so WCAG 2.5.7 is satisfied by construction. The loading plot is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table of every loading, communality and salience decision; markers are labelled by name on the plot itself and the two axes are distinguished by dash pattern as well as colour. Sliders announce meaningful values ('axes 55 degrees apart, oblique solution, factors correlate 0.57'). An invariants box states in words what has not changed after each rotation. Reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Factor analysis: what rotation changes, what it cannot change, and why simple structure is a criterion rather than a discovery
tools.simulationNotes: Three fictional marker sets with coordinates chosen to make three situations legible: a clean two-cluster structure, one containing a genuine cross-loading, and one whose clusters sit about 55 degrees apart. No correlation matrix was factored and no real study is represented. Rotation is applied as a coordinate transform; oblique solutions read loadings against non-perpendicular axes and report the implied factor correlation as the cosine of the angle between them. Pattern and structure coefficients are not distinguished, the number of factors is fixed at two, and the 'find the simplest structure' control is a coarse sweep rather than varimax, oblimin or promax.

tools.title: Facet-Level Detective
tools.summary: Two fictional people share a broad domain score almost exactly and behave quite differently. Students assign behavioural evidence before the facet scores are shown, build their own matched pair, then watch the "fixed" broad score reverse its ranking when the questionnaire samples facets differently.
learningObjectives: Explain why a broad domain score, being an average of narrower facets, cannot distinguish two people who reach it from opposite directions.
Predict specific behaviour from facet scores rather than from a domain score, and say why the domain score cannot do that job.
State the bandwidth-fidelity trade-off: broad predictors suit broad outcomes, narrow predictors suit narrow ones.
Describe why the facet level is less settled and less reliably measured than the domain level.
Explain how a domain score depends on the questionnaire's item sampling as well as on the person.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout using native radios, selects, ranges and buttons; each observation is a fieldset whose legend carries the behaviour, so options are never announced orphaned; charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired with visible tables carrying the same numbers, and every bar prints its own value; verdict tone stated in words as well as by border colour; changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Trait structure: what a broad domain score averages away, and the bandwidth-fidelity trade-off
tools.simulationNotes: All people and scores are fictional, on an arbitrary 0-100 scale with no norms, no standard error and no reference sample. A domain score is modelled as the weighted mean of two facet scores; behavioural tendency is a linear function of facet scores with no error, no situational input and no trait interaction. Facet pair names are taken from a published two-aspect account of the Big Five so that students learn vocabulary that exists, but no published item, norm or finding is reproduced.

tools.title: The Alpha Trap
tools.summary: Students maximise Cronbach's alpha by choosing items from a simulated bank, discover that the cheapest route is to ask the same question five ways, and then see the narrow scale they have built fail against a simulated outcome.
learningObjectives: Explain why Cronbach's alpha rises with both the number of items and their average intercorrelation, and why neither is a property of the construct.
Explain why a high alpha is not evidence of unidimensionality.
Explain why a high alpha is not evidence of validity, using the bloated specific factor as the mechanism.
Judge a scale on content coverage and item redundancy rather than on its reliability coefficient alone.
Recognise that a very high alpha in a short scale is a warning about item redundancy rather than a mark of quality.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout using native checkboxes, radios and buttons; the coverage chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible data table carrying the same numbers; state changes announced through the shell's polite live region; redundancy and outcome verdicts state their tone in words as well as by border colour; stage progress carried by aria-current and visible text; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Reliability: why a high Cronbach's alpha is not validity, unidimensionality or evidence of a good measure
tools.itemSource: All 24 items were written for this tool. No published or commercial questionnaire is reproduced, in whole or in part.
tools.simulationNotes: Every figure is the value implied by a fictional correlation model, not an estimate from a sample. Items load on a general factor, a content-area factor and, for near-duplicates, a wording-specific factor; the simulated outcome responds to the general factor and to breadth of coverage but not to wording. No sampling error is modelled, so no confidence intervals are shown. The construct and its five content areas are invented for teaching.

tools.title: Response-Style Simulator
tools.summary: Seven fictional respondents with the same true standing answer the same twenty items in seven different ways. Students compare raw grids, distributions, totals and split-half correlations, watch balanced keying neutralise acquiescence and unbalanced keying disguise it, then identify a mystery pattern and are asked what it cannot tell them.
learningObjectives: Recognise acquiescent, extreme, midpoint, impression-managed, random, straight-lined and attentive response patterns from their evidence.
Explain why balanced keying neutralises acquiescence and why an unbalanced scale cannot distinguish it from a high score.
Explain why a total score reflects how a person uses a rating scale as well as the trait.
State what a response pattern can establish and what it cannot.
Frame a data-screening decision as a stated methodological choice rather than a judgement about respondents.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Every answer is printed as its own digit inside its cell, so a response grid is readable as text and the shading is a redundant cue rather than the carrier. Reverse-keyed items are marked with a dotted underline and described in the text, never by colour alone. The distribution chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible summary table. Native checkboxes, radios, range and number inputs throughout; sliders announce meaningful values. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Response styles: what a rating pattern shows, why balanced keying matters, and what no pattern can establish about a motive
tools.simulationNotes: Seven fictional respondents sharing one true standing on an unnamed trait, answering twenty generated items on a 1-5 scale. Each style is a transformation of the same underlying response. Randomness uses a seeded mulberry32 generator with the seed shown and settable. No real questionnaire, item or dataset is reproduced. Styles are modelled as pure and constant, which real respondents are not; detection uses five simple summary statistics rather than long-string indices, person-fit statistics or response latencies. Impression management is modelled as a shift towards the desirable end and is explicitly not a measure of deception. The tool never attributes a motive to a pattern and marks any answer that does as overreaching.

tools.title: “Explain This Person” Courtroom
tools.summary: One fictional behaviour and eight explanations that all fit it. Students rate each, request evidence, and discover that fitting a case is cheap while predicting something distinctive is not. The verdict rewards evidence that discriminates and proportionate confidence, and scores down anyone who converges on a single cause.
learningObjectives: Explain what underdetermination means for psychological explanation.
Distinguish an explanation that accommodates a behaviour from one that predicts something distinctive.
Identify what evidence would discriminate between two accounts that both fit.
Distinguish competing explanations from compatible ones.
Calibrate confidence to what the available evidence can support.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Each explanation is a fieldset whose floated legend carries the full statement, so rating options are never announced orphaned; the floated legend also prevents multi-line legends spilling out of their box. Native radios, checkboxes and buttons throughout. The competition diagram is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table stating every pair's relationship in words; nodes are labelled and supported/undermined states are conveyed by stroke pattern as well as fill. Requirements tick off in a live checklist with '(met)' / '(not yet)' in the text. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Explanation and underdetermination: why fitting a case is cheap and predicting something distinctive is not
tools.simulationNotes: A fictional case with eight explanations written to be compatible with it, and six pieces of evidence whose findings are stipulated. There is no correct answer and none is stored: the tool has no hidden fact about why the fictional person acted. Explanations are scored on fit and on how much their predictions differ from rivals'; the verdict responds to whether discriminating evidence was requested, whether confidence is proportionate, and whether compatible explanations were kept alive. Distinctiveness is not truth, and the page says so.

tools.title: Intelligence-Test Battery Builder
tools.summary: Seven generic cognitive task families, one testing session, and three different purposes. Students assemble a battery under time and burden constraints, watch breadth, reliability, exposure-dependence and burden trade against each other, then see the same battery judged against all three purposes without a single task changing.
learningObjectives: Explain why validity is a property of a stated use rather than of a test.
Name the constraints that assembling a battery forces into conflict: time, breadth, reliability, exposure-dependence and burden.
Explain why composite reliability rises with test length almost regardless of what is measured, and why that makes it weak evidence of quality.
Explain why removing language from a task reduces some demands without making it independent of prior experience.
Justify a battery against a stated purpose rather than in the abstract.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native checkboxes, select and buttons throughout; each task card carries its costs as text so nothing depends on inspecting a chart. The coverage chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table that states 'not sampled' and 'barely' in words as well as by bar length. Requirements tick off in a live checklist with '(met)' / '(not yet)' written into the text. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Intelligence testing: construct coverage, the trade-offs in battery construction, and validity as a property of a use
tools.simulationNotes: Seven generic task families described in general terms; no published test, subtest, item, norm or scoring rule is reproduced, and no test is named. All values (minutes, reliability, breadth weights, exposure-dependence, burden) are illustrative and were written for this tool. Composite reliability uses Spearman-Brown on the mean task reliability and ignores intercorrelations. 'Fit to purpose' is a weighted sum invented for this tool and is not a recognised index. The tool scores batteries only: it produces no ability score for any person and simulates no group differences of any kind. Exposure-dependence is a property of a task's reliance on prior opportunity to learn its content and is never attached to a person or population.

tools.title: Culture-Fair Test Challenge
tools.summary: Students design a non-verbal reasoning task through six decisions and watch six construct-irrelevant demands respond. Removing language removes one of them. Four fictional participants, described only by prior experience of testing formats, show how unevenly a design distributes demands that have nothing to do with reasoning.
learningObjectives: Explain why removing language from a test removes the reading demand and leaves the others intact.
Distinguish construct-relevant from construct-irrelevant demands, and use that framing instead of 'culture-free'.
Explain opportunity to learn a test format as a fact about exposure rather than about capacity.
State what evidence is required before scores from different groups can be treated as comparable.
Recognise that reducing construct-irrelevant demand costs administration time, and is a design decision rather than a discovered property.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native radios, checkboxes and buttons throughout; each design option carries its consequence as text beneath the label. The demand chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table rating each demand 'high', 'moderate' or 'low' in words. The construct-share bar prints its own labels and percentages inside each segment and repeats them in the note beneath, so the split never depends on the fill colours. Participant cards state the load as text as well as showing a meter. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Culture-fair testing: construct-irrelevant demand, opportunity to learn a format, and what comparability requires
tools.simulationNotes: A design model with illustrative values written for this tool; no published test is described. Six construct-irrelevant demands are tracked, combined by maximum rather than sum, and converted to a construct-relevant share by a simple linear rule. The four fictional participants are characterised ONLY by prior experience of testing formats, devices and puzzle conventions: no nationality, ethnicity, region, language or group membership appears anywhere in the tool, and no group difference of any kind is simulated. The tool produces no score, ability estimate or performance prediction for any person, fictional or real; the participant figure is a count of demands the design makes that the person has not had opportunity to become familiar with, and the page states this explicitly wherever it appears.

tools.title: Twin-Study Simulator
tools.summary: Students set the true variance components, generate fictional twin and sibling pairs from them, and recover ACE estimates with Falconer's formulae — then switch on unequal environments, assortative mating and gene-environment correlation and watch the estimates fail in opposite directions while the truth stays put.
learningObjectives: State what heritability is a property of: variance in a population under particular environmental conditions.
Explain why heritability says nothing about the causes of any individual's trait, and nothing about malleability.
Derive ACE estimates from MZ and DZ correlations using Falconer's formulae.
Name the assumptions the derivation rests on and say which direction each violation biases the estimate.
Explain why equalising environments raises heritability without any genetic change.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person or their family.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, number input and buttons throughout; every slider announces a meaningful value ('assumption held' rather than '0'). The three scatterplots are hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table of pair counts and correlations, and each panel's correlation is also printed as text. The truth-against-estimate table labels every discrepancy 'overestimate', 'underestimate' or 'close' in words. The random seed is exposed so a demonstration is exactly reproducible. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Behaviour genetics: what heritability is a property of, and which way each broken assumption bends the estimate
tools.simulationNotes: Fictional pairs from a seeded mulberry32 generator; 250 pairs per group. Phenotype is a*A + c*C + e*E + m*M with independent standard-normal sources; pair resemblance is produced by the proportion of A and C the pair shares. Estimates use Falconer's formulae. No trait is named and no real study, family or dataset is represented. The model is purely additive: no dominance, epistasis, sex differences, age moderation or gene-environment interaction (gene-environment correlation is modelled). No group comparison of any kind is simulated, and the simulation contains a single undifferentiated population.

tools.title: Gene × Environment Interaction Visualiser
tools.summary: Students name the pattern in a study that sampled only the adverse half of an environmental range, then watch the range widen and the same two groups turn a diathesis-stress finding into differential susceptibility. An explorer then lets them move slopes, crossover and sampled window and see which theory the visible data appear to support.
learningObjectives: Distinguish diathesis-stress, differential susceptibility and vantage sensitivity by the location of the crossover point.
Explain why the range of environments a study sampled can decide which of the three theories it appears to support.
Explain why a significant interaction term does not choose between the three.
State what evidence is needed to claim differential susceptibility rather than vulnerability.
Describe sensitivity as responsiveness in both directions rather than as a defect.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, checkboxes and buttons throughout; sliders announce meaningful values such as 'crossover inside the range'. Charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table giving both groups' model-implied outcomes and their difference at three points in the sampled range. The two groups are distinguished by colour, by dash pattern and by a label printed at the end of each line. The pattern the visible data support is stated in words in a live verdict box. Unsampled regions are shaded and described in the readout as a percentage of range sampled. Reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Gene-environment interaction: how the sampled environmental range decides which theory a study appears to support
tools.simulationNotes: Two fictional sensitivity groups, each a straight line in environmental quality with normally distributed noise, generated from a seeded mulberry32 generator. No gene is named and no genotype appears: the grouping variable is a fictional sensitivity score split for display. No disorder, diagnosis, symptom or clinical risk estimate is used and the outcome axis is an unnamed standardised outcome. No value corresponds to any published finding. Straight lines and a two-group split are deliberate simplifications, both stated on the page; no sampling uncertainty or confidence band is shown.
